profiles.focus: Use the girls’ growth chart to follow weight and length over time. Feeding and vitamin requirements at this age are not different solely because of sex.
food: Feed breast milk or iron-fortified infant formula responsively; hunger and fullness cues guide quantity. Do not dilute formula.
Around 6 months, when developmentally ready, introduce soft iron-rich foods such as puréed meat, lentils or iron-fortified cereal. Offer varied textures safely; no honey before 12 months.
supplements: Breastfed or partly breastfed infants: vitamin D 400 IU (10 mcg) daily from the first days of life. Ask about drops if formula intake is insufficient to provide this amount.
Iron supplements require pediatric guidance, especially for prematurity or exclusive breastfeeding. Do not use adult multivitamins or guess an iron dose.
move: Provide supervised floor play several times daily. Before independent mobility, aim for at least 30 minutes of tummy time daily, divided into short awake sessions.
Encourage reaching and crawling as development allows. Always place babies on their backs for sleep; no sex-specific exercise quota is supported.

profiles.focus: Use the boys’ growth chart to follow weight and length over time. Feeding and vitamin requirements at this age are not different solely because of sex.
food: Feed breast milk or iron-fortified infant formula responsively; hunger and fullness cues guide quantity. Do not dilute formula.
Around 6 months, when developmentally ready, introduce soft iron-rich foods such as puréed meat, lentils or iron-fortified cereal. Offer varied textures safely; no honey before 12 months.
supplements: Breastfed or partly breastfed infants: vitamin D 400 IU (10 mcg) daily from the first days of life. Ask about drops if formula intake is insufficient to provide this amount.
Iron supplements require pediatric guidance, especially for prematurity or exclusive breastfeeding. Do not use adult multivitamins or guess an iron dose.
move: Provide supervised floor play several times daily. Before independent mobility, aim for at least 30 minutes of tummy time daily, divided into short awake sessions.
Encourage reaching and crawling as development allows. Always place babies on their backs for sleep; no sex-specific exercise quota is supported.

profiles.focus: Follow an age- and sex-specific growth chart for girls; avoid comparing portions with another child. Before puberty, nutrient and activity targets are generally shared.
food: Offer regular meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, eggs, fish or other proteins. Water replaces sugary drinks; adults choose the food and children respond to appetite.
Calcium-rich choices include milk, yogurt and calcium-fortified alternatives. Daily calcium targets: 700 mg at 1–3, 1,000 mg at 4–8 and 1,300 mg at age 9.
supplements: Vitamin D target: 600 IU (15 mcg) daily from food and supplements combined. Consider a child-appropriate supplement if fortified foods do not meet needs.
Restricted or vegan diets need assessment for B12 and other gaps. Use iron only for an assessed need; keep all iron products out of children’s reach.
move: Ages 1–2: at least 180 minutes of varied movement daily. Ages 3–4: 180 minutes, including at least 60 minutes of energetic play.
Ages 5–9: average 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous activity across the week. Running, jumping and climbing can strengthen muscle and bone on at least 3 days weekly.

profiles.focus: Follow an age- and sex-specific growth chart for boys; avoid comparing portions with another child. Before puberty, nutrient and activity targets are generally shared.
food: Offer regular meals with vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, eggs, fish or other proteins. Water replaces sugary drinks; adults choose the food and children respond to appetite.
Calcium-rich choices include milk, yogurt and calcium-fortified alternatives. Daily calcium targets: 700 mg at 1–3, 1,000 mg at 4–8 and 1,300 mg at age 9.
supplements: Vitamin D target: 600 IU (15 mcg) daily from food and supplements combined. Consider a child-appropriate supplement if fortified foods do not meet needs.
Restricted or vegan diets need assessment for B12 and other gaps. Use iron only for an assessed need; keep all iron products out of children’s reach.
move: Ages 1–2: at least 180 minutes of varied movement daily. Ages 3–4: 180 minutes, including at least 60 minutes of energetic play.
Ages 5–9: average 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous activity across the week. Running, jumping and climbing can strengthen muscle and bone on at least 3 days weekly.

profiles.focus: Menstruation and rapid growth can increase iron needs. Heavy periods, persistent fatigue or missed periods during intense training deserve clinical review.
food: Eat enough to support growth and sport; include meals rather than skipping them. Pair beans or lentils with vitamin-C-rich fruit or vegetables.
Iron targets: 8 mg/day at 10–13 and 15 mg/day at 14–17. Calcium: 1,300 mg/day. These are total dietary targets, not supplement doses.
supplements: Vitamin D: 600 IU/day total. Use a supplement for dietary shortfalls; an iron supplement should follow assessment of iron status and menstrual losses.
For a vegan diet, obtain B12 reliably from fortified foods or supplements. If pregnancy is possible, discuss folic acid and reproductive-health needs with a clinician.
move: Average at least 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous activity. Include vigorous exercise plus muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days weekly.
Try brisk walking, cycling, dance or sport plus supervised strength work. Avoid training through pain or compensating for food with exercise.

profiles.focus: Rapid growth and demanding sport can increase energy needs. Build strength with food, recovery and supervised training rather than bodybuilding products.
food: Include a protein food at meals and enough grains, potatoes or other carbohydrates for training. Match extra portions to appetite and activity, not a fixed “male” serving.
Iron targets: 8 mg/day at 10–13 and 11 mg/day at 14–17. Calcium: 1,300 mg/day. Avoid restrictive cutting diets during growth.
supplements: Vitamin D: 600 IU/day total; consider supplementation for a dietary gap. B12 needs a reliable fortified-food or supplement source in vegan diets.
Do not take iron without assessment. Muscle-building supplements are not a replacement for meals; review any product with a qualified clinician.
move: Average at least 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous activity. Vigorous, muscle- and bone-strengthening activity belongs on at least 3 days weekly.
Choose enjoyable sport, swimming or cycling, with supervised resistance training and jumping. Technique and gradual progression matter more than maximal loads.

profiles.focus: Menstruation, pregnancy, breastfeeding and menopause require different nutrition plans; use the branch that applies to you.
food: Build meals around vegetables, whole grains, legumes and varied proteins. Include calcium-rich foods; age 18 needs 1,300 mg/day, ages 19–50 need 1,000 mg and 51–64 need 1,200 mg.
Iron: 15 mg/day at age 18, 18 mg at 19–50 and 8 mg at 51+. Pregnancy raises the target to 27 mg; heavy menstrual loss warrants assessment.
supplements: If pregnancy is possible, obtain 400 mcg/day folic acid from supplements, fortified foods or both, in addition to dietary folate. Prenatal needs require a separate clinical plan.
Vitamin D: 600 IU/day total. Supplement calcium only to cover a shortfall. Vegans need a reliable B12 source; avoid stacking overlapping multivitamins.
move: Weekly: 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity or 75–150 vigorous minutes, plus major-muscle strengthening at least 2 days.

Practical start: brisk walk 30 minutes on 5 days, plus 2 strength sessions. During uncomplicated pregnancy, aim for at least 150 moderate minutes weekly with obstetric guidance; adapt postpartum recovery individually.

profiles.focus: Focus on cardiovascular fitness, sustainable strength and adequate nutrition. Routine extra iron or testosterone-boosting supplements are not established necessities.
food: Choose vegetables, legumes, whole grains and varied proteins. Reduce salty processed foods; portions depend on body size and activity.
Iron: 11 mg/day at age 18 and 8 mg at 19+. Calcium: 1,300 mg at age 18, then 1,000 mg through age 64. A protein food at each meal can support strength training.
supplements: Vitamin D: 600 IU/day total. Supplement identified dietary gaps; obtain B12 reliably if vegan.
Avoid routine iron unless deficiency is established. Discuss supplement interactions and kidney disease before using concentrated products; a multivitamin does not replace a balanced diet.
move: Weekly: 150–300 moderate aerobic minutes or 75–150 vigorous minutes, plus strength for major muscle groups at least 2 days.
Example: brisk walk or cycle 30 minutes on 5 days, plus 2 strength sessions. Start gradually, vary intensity and break up prolonged sitting.

profiles.focus: After menopause, prioritize bone health, muscle maintenance and fall prevention; nutrition supplements do not replace osteoporosis evaluation.
food: Include protein at meals, fiber-rich plants and regular fluids. Unintentional weight loss or swallowing difficulties need review.
Calcium target: 1,200 mg/day. Iron: 8 mg/day. Combine food and fortified options before adding a calcium supplement.
supplements: Vitamin D: 600 IU/day at 65–70, 800 IU at 71+. A supplement can fill a dietary gap; osteoporosis treatment and dosing are individualized.
B12 absorption can decline with age: fortified foods or supplements may help. Review medication interactions and avoid assuming all anemia is iron deficiency.
move: As ability allows: 150–300 moderate aerobic minutes weekly and strength on at least 2 days. Shorter sessions count; some activity is better than none.

Balance and functional strength on at least 3 days weekly: supported single-leg stands, sit-to-stand practice or tai chi. A sample week is five 30-minute walks, two strength sessions and three short balance sessions.

profiles.focus: Maintain strength and balance; bone loss also affects men. Calcium needs change again after age 70.
food: Include protein at each meal, vegetables, beans and whole grains. Adapt texture and hydration to swallowing, dental and medical needs.
Calcium: 1,000 mg/day at 65–70 and 1,200 mg at 71+. Iron: 8 mg/day. Investigate unexplained weight loss or anemia rather than self-treating.
supplements: Vitamin D: 600 IU/day at 65–70, 800 IU at 71+. Consider calcium only for the portion missing from the diet.
Review B12 intake and absorption, especially with a restricted diet. Supplements require medication review; routine iron is not recommended without an established need.
move: As ability allows: 150–300 moderate aerobic minutes weekly, strength at least 2 days and balance/functional strength at least 3 days.
Try walking or stationary cycling, resistance bands, chair rises and supported balance practice. Build from short sessions; seek an adapted program if falls or mobility problems are present.
